extracted.intended_audience: journalists, reporters and editors producing news coverage
extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide listing preferred terms, discouraged usages, definitions and reporting guidance for covering diverse communities, identities, religions, disabilities and related topics. Intended to guide word choice, capitalization and sensitive framing in news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: incarcerated people
rubrics_metrics.description: Use constructions that include “person” or “people,” a subject’s name and/or fixed biographical characteristics when referring to people confined in correctional facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred examples: "incarcerated people", "imprisoned people", "people in prison", "people in jail", "people jailed in X facility", "formerly incarcerated people", "John Doe, who was incarcerated at FCI Memphis", "Jane Doe, who is serving 12 years in FCI Dublin", "A 34-year-old detained in Los Angeles County Jail", "Imprisoned in 1989, Joe Doe has filed an appeal." Use people-first and specific biographical detail rather than dehumanizing labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: inner city
rubrics_metrics.description: The term has been used as a euphemism for lower-income residential districts and sometimes to refer to Black neighborhoods; it can be imprecise and charged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral geographic adjectives like "city center", "downtown" or "central urban" for location; use "under-resourced" or "low-income" when referring to neighborhoods with high poverty. Avoid using inner city as a stand-in for race or poverty without specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: insane asylum/mental health hospital/psychiatric hospital
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical term 'insane asylum' is objectionable and inaccurate for hospitals that treat people with mental illnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer "mental health hospital" or "psychiatric hospital" to describe medical facilities devoted to treating people with mental disabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: insane, incompetent
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like insane, insanity and mentally deranged are informal and can be offensive; 'insanity' is a legal term in U.S. criminal law, not medical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use "mental illness" or "mental disorder" rather than "insane" or "mentally deranged," except in quotes or when referring to a criminal defense. Medical profession favors "mental disorder" or "psychopathology."

rubrics_metrics.name: inscrutable
rubrics_metrics.description: A synonym for mysterious that is considered racially charged, particularly when used to describe Asians or Asian Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution; avoid using this adjective in contexts that may carry racialized connotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: institutional racism
rubrics_metrics.description: When policies and practices put people who are not of the dominant race at a disadvantage across institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how structures, policies or practices disadvantage groups (housing policies, hiring, school discipline). Note that calling an institution racist may refer to structures rather than intent. See also 'systemic racism' and 'White privilege.' Provide concrete examples (e.g., school-to-prison pipeline).

rubrics_metrics.name: intellectual disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability involving significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior, typically developing before age 18; IQ of 75 or lower often considered intellectually disabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use people-first language: say "a person with an intellectual disability" rather than labeling someone "intellectually disabled." Contrast with congenital disorders such as Down syndrome.

rubrics_metrics.name: intelligent design
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that some life forms are so complex they reflect design by a conscious intelligence; proponents often imply God and reject evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe proponents' positions accurately (some reject common ancestry). Note overlap with creationism and how proponents do or do not identify a designer.

rubrics_metrics.name: interdenominational
rubrics_metrics.description: A congregation or organization formally approved or under the jurisdiction of more than one denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use as a synonym for 'nondenominational.' Use the term only when multiple denominations are formally involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: interfaith
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to activities or events that draw people from entirely different religious traditions (e.g., Christians, Jews, Buddhists, Muslims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a synonym for 'ecumenical,' which refers to multiple Christian traditions. Use 'interfaith' for cross-religion gatherings.

rubrics_metrics.name: internment, Japanese
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the WWII incarceration of 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry in the U.S.; many advocates prefer 'incarceration' instead of 'internment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note forced sales of homes/businesses and that most internees were released in 1946. Link to resources like the Japanese American National Museum for further info. Use 'incarceration' where more accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: interpreters
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution regarding using family members as interpreters for interview subjects with limited English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family members may produce flawed translations or withhold/alter content. If possible and time permits, have an independent native speaker review recordings or provide interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: intersectionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A lens recognizing that identities (gender, race, class, sexual orientation, etc.) interact and cannot be examined in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concept to clarify overlapping privilege and oppression (e.g., a White gay man may experience both). Apply in analysis and reporting when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: intersex (adj.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Umbrella term for people born with reproductive/sexual anatomy or chromosome patterns not classified as typically male or female; sometimes called Differences of Sex Development (DSD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the outdated/derogatory term 'hermaphrodite.' Do not conflate intersex with transgender; they are separate though some individuals may identify as both.

rubrics_metrics.name: intifada
rubrics_metrics.description: An Arabic term meaning shaking, uprising, insurrection; commonly used for Palestinian resistance to Israeli occupation of Gaza and the West Bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize there are distinct intifadas marked by specific events; use the term in its historical and political context.

rubrics_metrics.name: invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical term for a person debilitated by illness or injury; now widely viewed as offensive when applied to people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'invalid' to describe a person with a disability except in quotes; it implies lack of ability and is imprecise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iranian names
rubrics_metrics.description: Persian/Iranian names typically consist of a given name (sometimes more than one) followed by a family name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of order and cultural specifics; note examples such as names appearing in literature like Alf Layla wa-Layla. Use correct spelling and ordering per context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Islam
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion founded in seventh-century Mecca; followers are Muslims; major branches include Sunni and Shiite; no single central religious authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize Islamic titles when used before names and lowercase otherwise. Use title + name on first reference and last name after that. Be precise about Sunni/Shiite distinctions and titles (imam, sheikh, ayatollah, mufti, marja, etc.). Avoid assuming Arabs = Muslims or Muslims = Arabs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Islamic (adj.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective describing the religion of Islam; not synonymous with 'Islamist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Islamic' for religion-related descriptors and 'Muslim' as the noun for individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Islamic fundamentalist
rubrics_metrics.description: An American-constructed term implying political conservatism and sometimes extremism when applied to Muslims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful reporting should not assume religion is the sole basis for political actions. Attribute political actions to responsible groups or governments rather than the religion. Avoid stereotyping and constructions like 'Muslim bomb.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Islamist
rubrics_metrics.description: Per AP style: an advocate/supporter of a political movement favoring reordering government/society according to laws prescribed by Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use as a synonym for fighters, militants, extremists or radicals; be specific about militant affiliations when possible (e.g., al-Qaida-linked, Hezbollah, Taliban). Note that 'Islamists' span a broad range from mainstream politicians to militants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Islamophobia
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and prejudice against Muslims based on ideas that Islam is inferior or incompatible with modernity; predates 9/11 but has increased since.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize with data when relevant (e.g., Gallup reports on discrimination). Use accurate sourcing when reporting on anti-Muslim sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issei, issei
rubrics_metrics.description: Term for Japanese immigrants (first generation) with context-sensitive capitalization conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some institutions capitalize generational terms in generational contexts and lowercase when referring to an individual. Be consistent and follow institutional practice where relevant. See related terms Nisei, Sansei, Yonsei.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jainism
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion established in India in 6th century B.C. emphasizing nonviolence and renunciation; does not believe in a creator god.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide basic doctrinal points accurately (nonviolence, souls in plants/animals), and historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jap
rubrics_metrics.description: Derogatory slur originating in WWII-era usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid this term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japanese names
rubrics_metrics.description: In Japan family name typically comes first followed by personal name; in U.S. contexts Western order is common; many women's names end in -ko.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect cultural ordering and use Western order when appropriate for U.S. contexts. Be mindful of name elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jehovah's Witness
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious group using the name Jehovah for God, rejecting Trinity and some mainstream Christian classifications; they do not salute the flag or bear arms and refuse blood transfusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Kingdom Halls' for their gathering places; they have no formal clergy titles and do not use 'Rev.' Refer to baptized evangelizers as 'publishers' and other internal terms correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jew
rubrics_metrics.description: Follower of the Jewish faith; use as noun/adjective and capitalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Jew' for men and women. Never use 'jew' as a verb (e.g., 'he jewed me down')—that is offensive. Be mindful of cultural/ethnic vs. religious uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jews for Jesus
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper name of an organization founded by Jews who converted to evangelical Christianity; part of Messianic Judaism movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not group them with mainstream Jews; clearly state they are Christian by faith though Jewish by culture/ethnicity. Treat the organization as distinct from mainstream Jewish groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: jihad
rubrics_metrics.description: Arabic word meaning 'struggle' or 'striving'; traditionally inward spiritual struggle but has also been used for defensive military action; militant usage has sometimes implied 'holy war' though that is not literal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid translating it simplistically as 'holy war'; note traditional and modern usages and that majority of Muslims do not use it to mean 'holy war.' Provide context when reporting on militant invocations of the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jim Crow
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws enforcing strict segregation between black and white people, primarily in the American South, used to justify nearly 80 years of segregation and disenfranchisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide historical context including origins (minstrel routine by Daddy Rice) and effects on daily life (segregation in schools, transportation, public amenities). Cite historians or authoritative sources where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judaism
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion of the Jewish people with a 4,000-year history; includes branches such as Reform, Orthodox and Conservative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing branches, note distinguishing practices and institutions (Reform's adaptability; Orthodox adherence; Conservative middle path; Reconstructionist and Renewal movements). Use correct capitalization and organizational names on first and second references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juneteenth
rubrics_metrics.description: Oldest known celebration commemorating the end of slavery in the U.S., originating in Galveston, Texas, June 19, 1865.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe it as a day/week/month of celebration emphasizing freedom, education and achievement; note common observances (speakers, picnics, gatherings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kaaba
rubrics_metrics.description: The black, cube-shaped building in Mecca central to Islamic worship; pilgrims circle it on hajj and face it in prayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred spelling 'Kaaba' and pronunciation guidance; explain its religious significance and physical description (black stone in eastern corner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kabbalah
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient Jewish mystical doctrine; preferred spelling 'Kabbalah' and uppercase in all references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe its basic aims (understanding divine mysteries) and historical prominence; capitalize consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: kafiyyeh
rubrics_metrics.description: A checked scarf-like garment worn on the head by some Arab men; traditional and cultural rather than religious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May also be spelled keffiyeh or kufiya. Note that styles/colors can have significance and the garment expresses cultural identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: karaoke
rubrics_metrics.description: Originated in Japan in the 1970s, meaning 'empty orchestra'; patrons sing along to instrumental recordings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the social and cultural origins and that it spread to other Asian countries and to the U.S. in the 1990s.

rubrics_metrics.name: karma
rubrics_metrics.description: In Buddhism and Hinduism, the universal law of cause and effect; the effect of a person's actions in their next lifetime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowercase in all references; explain the religious-philosophical meaning when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kashrut
rubrics_metrics.description: Body of Jewish law governing what foods are permitted and how they must be prepared; root relates to 'fit' or 'proper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to 'kosher' as the common term describing food that meets these standards. Use 'kashrut' when discussing the legal system or laws; link to 'kosher.'

rubrics_metrics.name: keloid
rubrics_metrics.description: A raised scar that can develop after skin injury; more likely in people of African or Asian descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide medical description of formation and prevalence; use neutral medical language.

rubrics_metrics.name: kesh
rubrics_metrics.description: The wearing of long uncut hair by Sikhs as one of the Five K’s (articles of faith) representing respect for God's creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain its religious significance and connection to Sikh observance (ordered by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699).

rubrics_metrics.name: killing fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally refers to sites of mass massacre in Cambodia by the Khmer Rouge; broadly can mean any site of mass killing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute the coining to Dith Pran and note the cultural reference to the film 'The Killing Fields.' Use with historical specificity when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: kippa, kippah
rubrics_metrics.description: See yarmulke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to entry for 'yarmulke' for preferred usage and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Koran
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Koran' is an alternate spelling; the preferred spelling is 'Quran' and it is capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Quran' in most references; reserve 'Koran' only if it appears in a specific title or name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Korean names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first followed by two-part personal name; many Korean Americans adopt Western name order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of order differences and gendered naming conventions; record and present names respecting individuals' preferences and cultural norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: kosher
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective meaning ritually permitted under Jewish dietary law; lowercase in all references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain connections to 'kashrut' when relevant. Use 'kosher' to describe food or ritual objects that meet standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ku Klux Klan
rubrics_metrics.description: Official name 'Knights of the Ku Klux Klan'; founded in 1915 and directed against blacks, Catholics, Jews and other groups; multiple separate organizations exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full name on first reference; KKK initials acceptable on second reference. Capitalize formal titles before a name (e.g., Imperial Wizard). Refer to members as Klansmen or Klanswomen.

rubrics_metrics.name: kufi
rubrics_metrics.description: A skullcap worn by some Muslims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term when describing headwear; be precise about cultural/religious contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kwanzaa
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebration of African heritage and principles occurring Dec. 26–Jan. 1, created in the 1960s; emphasizes seven principles and symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the seven principles (umoja, kujichagulia, ujima, ujamaa, nia, kuumba, imani) and seven symbols. Note it was intended to be independent of religion though some families incorporate religious holidays. Link to official Kwanzaa site for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: lama
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tibetan Buddhist teacher or master; capitalize when used as a title before a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize as a title (e.g., Lama Surya Das) and capitalize 'Dalai Lama' as an honorific title.

rubrics_metrics.name: lame
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly used to describe difficulty walking from leg injury but can be objectionable when applied to people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'lame' to describe a person except in quotes; choose precise, non-derogatory language when describing physical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laotian names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first and personal name second; often multi-syllable names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of order and complexity; record names respectfully and accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin@
rubrics_metrics.description: A post-internet construction simplifying Latino/Latina by using @; used by some academic departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the @ ending as offering simultaneous presentation of feminine and masculine endings; refer to Chican@ for related forms. Use where appropriate to institution or audience conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latina/Latino
rubrics_metrics.description: Umbrella terms for U.S. residents/citizens with Latin American ancestry; Latina is feminine, Latino masculine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Latina(s) for women and Latino(s) for men. Note regional preferences (Latino commonly used west of the Mississippi). Federal policy defines 'Latino' as an ethnicity, not a race. See related entries (Chicana/Chicano, Latin@, Latine, Latinx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Latine
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender-neutral or non-binary alternative to Latino/Latina using the 'e' ending; originated in Spanish-speaking, LGBTQIA+ and feminist communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciation la-TEEN-eh; increasingly used and easier to pronounce than Latinx. Use according to communities' preferences and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latinx
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender-neutral alternative to Latino/Latina using -x; pronounced 'La-teen-ex' and plural often 'Latinxs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware many Hispanic/Latino people are unfamiliar with or do not use the term; cite survey data (Pew) showing limited adoption. Use when appropriate to audience or subject preferences and note alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latter-day Saints
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints', 'LDS Church', 'Mormon'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow preferred usage and capitalization from the church when relevant; consider organization-preferred references.

rubrics_metrics.name: lay person
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of the laity rather than the clergy; 'lay person' and 'lay people' are two words; 'layman' and 'laywoman' are each one word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct spacing and gendered forms where appropriate; prefer gender-neutral forms when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: LDS Church
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable on second reference for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; 'church' is lowercase when using the shortened term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'LDS Church' on second reference; lowercase 'church' in the shortened form. Follow church's naming preferences on first reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lent
rubrics_metrics.description: Period of penance and fasting before Easter; observance varies across denominations and traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe timing and observance differences (begins Ash Wednesday, ends Holy Thursday in some calendars). Note fasting/abstinence norms and denominational variation; contextualize for accuracy when reporting on practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: lesbian
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred term for women attracted to other women; can be noun or adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some women prefer 'gay'; when possible ask subjects which term they prefer.

rubrics_metrics.name: LGBT/GLBT/LGBTQ/LGBTQ+/LGBTQQIA*
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and usage of umbrella acronyms for sexual and gender minorities; LGBTQ+ recommended by this guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not refer to an individual as 'LGBT' or 'LGBTQ+'; use these as group descriptors. Note differing recommendations: NLGJA recommends 'LGBTQ+'; GLAAD recommends 'LGBTQ'; Diversity Style Guide recommends 'LGBTQ+'. Explain that the Q may mean 'questioning' or 'queer' and that '+' denotes additional identities. Use specific identities when possible and avoid treating the group as monolithic.

rubrics_metrics.name: lifestyle
rubrics_metrics.description: Inaccurate term sometimes used to describe lives of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'lifestyle' to describe sexual orientation; sexual orientation is not a 'lifestyle.' See 'sexual orientation' or 'sexual preference.'

rubrics_metrics.name: linguistic racism
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination based on accent, dialect or speech patterns that can be overt or covert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples (mocking accent, 'you speak English well for someone who looks like you'). Explain how certain languages/dialects are undervalued and name groups especially affected (Spanish speakers, AAVE). Use the term to describe systemic and interpersonal discrimination related to language.

rubrics_metrics.name: little person
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference: see dwarf, midget, short stature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the more specific entries (dwarf/short stature) for preferred terminology and people-first language; avoid derogatory terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: liturgy
rubrics_metrics.description: Has two sets of meanings: for Western Christians a standard set of prayers (lowercase), for Orthodox/Eastern contexts 'Liturgy' is capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lowercase for Western Christian usages; uppercase 'Liturgy' when referring to Orthodox Christians and Eastern Catholics. Be sensitive to denominational differences in terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lord
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize when referring to God in a monotheistic faith (e.g., Lord Jesus, Lord Krishna).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize 'Lord' in religious contexts referencing a deity.

rubrics_metrics.name: lover
rubrics_metrics.description: Term preferred by some for a sexual partner; alternatives include girlfriend, boyfriend, partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subject's preferred term; consider context and specificity when choosing romantic/sexual partner descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lubavitch, Lubavitcher
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hasidic movement (also called Chabad-Lubavitch) originating in Russia and influential in American Jewish life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain origins, leadership (Rebbe), and movement practices; note alternate names and affiliations and use preferred identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: lupus
rubrics_metrics.description: A chronic autoimmune disease that can affect many organs; disproportionately affects Black women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral medical descriptions and note demographic patterns where reliable sources indicate prevalence differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lutheran
rubrics_metrics.description: Member of a Protestant denomination tracing roots to Martin Luther; two major U.S. bodies are ELCA and Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing Lutherans, note denominational distinctions (ELCA more liberal; Missouri Synod more conservative) and institutional affiliations. Use correct capitalization and full names on first reference.
